claim: TMEM16A forms calcium-activated chloride channels (CaCCs) that regulate physiological processes such as the secretions of airway epithelia and exocrine glands, the contraction of smooth muscles, and the excitability of neurons.
source: TMEM16A forms calcium-activated chloride channels (CaCCs) that regulate physiological processes such as the secretions of airway epithelia and exocrine glands, the contraction of smooth muscles, and the excitability of neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about TMEM16A function as stated in the abstract.

claim: Four acidic amino acids are putative calcium-binding residues in TMEM16A.
source: By aligning distantly related calcium-activated ion channels in the TMEM16 family and conducting systematic mutagenesis of all conserved acidic residues thought to be exposed to the cytoplasm, we identify four acidic amino acids as putative calcium-binding residues.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from systematic mutagenesis and alignment studies described in the abstract.

claim: Alterations of the charge, polarity, and size of amino acid side chains at the four identified sites alter the ability of different divalent cations to activate TMEM16A.
source: Alterations of the charge, polarity, and size of amino acid side chains at these sites alter the ability of different divalent cations to activate the channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies described in the abstract.

claim: TMEM16A mutant channels containing double cysteine substitutions at the identified residues are sensitive to the redox potential of the internal solution.
source: Furthermore, TMEM16A mutant channels containing double cysteine substitutions at these residues are sensitive to the redox potential of the internal solution, providing evidence for their physical proximity and solvent accessibility.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from redox manipulation experiments described in the abstract.

claim: The sensitivity of TMEM16A mutant channels to redox potential provides evidence for the physical proximity and solvent accessibility of the identified residues.
source: Furthermore, TMEM16A mutant channels containing double cysteine substitutions at these residues are sensitive to the redox potential of the internal solution, providing evidence for their physical proximity and solvent accessibility.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the redox sensitivity data.

claim: TMEM16A and TMEM16B are calcium-activated chloride channels (CaCCs).
source: Transmembrane proteins of the TMEM16 family include a number of calcium-dependent ion channels, such as the TMEM16A (Caputo et al., 2008; Schroeder et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008b) and TMEM16B (Schroeder et al., 2008; Stöhr et al., 2009) calcium-activated chloride channels (CaCCs)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TMEM16F is a small conductance calcium-activated nonselective cation (SCAN) channel.
source: TMEM16F (Yang et al., 2012) small conductance calcium-activated nonselective cation (SCAN) channel
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: TMEM16 proteins have been implicated in the control of fluid secretion in epithelia.
source: These proteins have been implicated in a wide range of physiological activities (Hartzell et al., 2009; Kunzelmann et al., 2011; Berg et al., 2012; Scudieri et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2012a) including the control of fluid secretion in epithelia (Romanenko et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2012b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TMEM16 proteins have been implicated in the regulation of membrane excitability in neurons.
source: the regulation of membrane excitability in neurons (Billig et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2012c)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TMEM16 proteins have been implicated in the scrambling of membrane lipids in platelets.
source: the scrambling of membrane lipids in platelets (Suzuki et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TMEM16 proteins have been implicated in the metastasis of certain cancers.
source: the metastasis of certain cancers (Katoh, 2003; Duvvuri et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mechanism by which calcium activates TMEM16 proteins is still extensively debated.
source: Despite their important physiological roles, the mechanism by which calcium activates these proteins is still extensively debated.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the current state of the field.

claim: One proposed model for TMEM16A calcium sensitivity resembles that of small-conductance KCa (SK) channels, where calcium ions interact with calmodulin.
source: In one model resembling that of the small-conductance KCa (SK) channels (Xia et al., 1998; Schumacher et al., 2001), calcium ions interact with calmodulin (CaM), and the physical association of calmodulin with TMEM16A is required to transduce the free energy of ion–protein interaction into movements of the channel gate (Tian et al., 2011; Vocke et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies proposing this model.

claim: A second proposed model for TMEM16A calcium sensitivity resembles that of large-conductance KCa (BK) channels, where calcium binds directly to the channel.
source: In a second model similar to that of the large-conductance KCa (BK) channels (Schreiber and Salkoff, 1997; Shi et al., 2002; Xia et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2010; Yuan et al., 2010), calcium binds directly to TMEM16A, and this interaction drives channel activation (Yu et al., 2012, 2014; Terashima et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies proposing this model.

claim: Wildtype mouse TMEM16A-CaCC exhibits calcium-dependent activation with an EC50 of approximately 1.0 ± 0.1 μM at +60 mV.
source: Compared to wildtype (WT) channels (EC50: 1.0 ± 0.1 μM)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from inside-out patch clamp recordings.

claim: Co-expression of mutant CaM molecules without functional calcium-binding sites did not reduce the apparent calcium sensitivity of endogenous TMEM16A-CaCC in Xenopus oocytes.
source: We found that co-expression of mutant CaM molecules without functional calcium-binding sites in the N-terminal lobe (CaM12), C-terminal lobe (CaM34), or both lobes (CaM1234) did not reduce the apparent calcium sensitivity of the endogenous TMEM16A-CaCC in Xenopus oocytes (Figure 1D), in agreement with a recent study (Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and cited literature.

claim: Anti-CaM antibody applied to the cytoplasmic side of inside-out patches had no effect on TMEM16A-CaCC currents.
source: In contrast to its potent inhibitory effect on CaM-dependent TRPV1 tachyphylaxis (Lishko et al., 2007), the CaM-antibody had no effect on TMEM16A-CaCC currents (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Neither acute nor sustained applications of W7, a CaM antagonist, disrupted the calcium sensitivity of TMEM16A channels.
source: We found that neither acute nor sustained applications of this drug disrupted the calcium sensitivity of TMEM16A channels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Barium, a divalent cation that cannot bind to CaM, can potently activate TMEM16A channels in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Third, consistent with previous reports (Xiao et al., 2011; Yuan et al., 2013; Ni et al., 2014), we found that barium, a divalent cation that cannot bind to CaM (Chao et al., 1984), can still potently activate TMEM16A channels in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutating residues V310, Y314, and L319 reported to be necessary for CaM-TMEM16A interactions did not reduce the apparent calcium sensitivity of mouse TMEM16A channel.
source: Fourth, mutating three residues (V310, Y314, and L319) that were recently reported to be necessary for CaM-TMEM16A interactions (Vocke et al., 2013) did not reduce the apparent calcium sensitivity of the mouse TMEM16A channel expressed in HEK 293 cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: CaM is not responsible for the calcium sensitivity of TMEM16A-CaCCs.
source: Because we were unable to alter TMEM16A-CaCC activity by inhibiting CaM function, could activate TMEM16A-CaCCs with barium, and could not shift channel EC50 by mutating the putative CaM-TMEM16A binding interface, we conclude that CaM is not responsible for the calcium sensitivity of TMEM16A-CaCCs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results.

claim: E698Q and E701Q mutations greatly reduced the apparent calcium affinity of TMEM16A-CaCC.
source: We found that alanine substitutions at E698 and E701 greatly reduced the apparent calcium affinity of TMEM16A-CaCC (Figure 3), similar to the effects of glutamine substitutions at these residues (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The alanine mutagenesis screen identified three additional acidic residues (E650, E730, and D734) that were critical for the calcium sensitivity of TMEM16A channels.
source: Moreover, our screen identified three additional acidic residues (E650, E730, and D734) that were critical for the calcium sensitivity of TMEM16A channels (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Alanine mutations of E650, E730, and D734 resulted in at least a 10-fold reduction of apparent calcium sensitivity.
source: Similar to E698A and E701A, alanine mutations of these three acidic residues resulted in at least a 10-fold reduction of apparent calcium sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutagenesis screen.

claim: The five residues identified by the alanine mutagenesis screen are confined to the region between the fifth and seventh putative transmembrane segments.
source: Interestingly, these five residues identified by our screen are confined to the region between the fifth and seventh putative transmembrane segments (Figure 2C) (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2C and citation.

claim: Cysteine substitutions at E650, E698, E701, E730, and D734 reduced the apparent calcium sensitivity of TMEM16A channels.
source: Introduction of cysteine substitutions at these sites replaces the glutamate or aspartate side chain with a small, hydrophobic methyl sulfhydryl group. Understandably, these manipulations had effects comparable to those of alanine substitutions (Figure 3C) and reduced the apparent calcium sensitivity of the channel (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3C and 4F.

claim: E698R and E701R mutations increased EC50 by several thousand-fold to 5.0 ± 0.3 mM and 3.3 ± 0.5 mM, respectively.
source: Compared to wildtype (WT) channels (EC50: 1.0 ± 0.1 μM), the EC50s of E698R and E701R were increased by several thousand-fold to 5.0 ± 0.3 mM and 3.3 ± 0.5 mM, respectively
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: E730R mutation increased EC50 to 0.6 ± 0.3 mM.
source: while the effects of E730R were milder, increasing EC50 to 0.6 ± 0.3 mM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: D734R mutation elevated EC50 to such a great extent that 10 mM intracellular calcium was unable to activate the mutant channel.
source: The most substantial changes were caused by the D734R mutation, which elevated EC50 to such a great extent that 10 mM intracellular calcium, the highest concentration of calcium used in this study, was unable to activate the mutant channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: The lack of CaCC current in D734R mutants was not due to defects in protein expression or folding because cadmium ions could still robustly activate the channel.
source: The lack of CaCC current in D734R mutants was not due to defects in protein expression or folding because cadmium ions could still robustly activate the channel (see below).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cadmium activation data.

claim: E650R mutation only produced a small reduction in calcium sensitivity (EC50: 6.5 ± 0.8 µM).
source: In contrast, the arginine substitution in E650R mutants only produced a small reduction in calcium sensitivity (EC50: 6.5 ± 0.8 µM), suggesting that the side chain at position 650 may not be directly involved in calcium coordination.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: The side chain at position 650 may not be directly involved in calcium coordination.
source: In contrast, the arginine substitution in E650R mutants only produced a small reduction in calcium sensitivity (EC50: 6.5 ± 0.8 µM), suggesting that the side chain at position 650 may not be directly involved in calcium coordination.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from mutagenesis data.

claim: E698D and E701D mutations resulted in only a 3 to 10-fold increase in channel EC50 (3.3 ± 0.9 µM and 10.4 ± 3.4 µM, respectively).
source: Charge-preserving mutations in E698D and E701D resulted in only a 3 to 10-fold increase in channel EC50 (3.3 ± 0.9 µM and 10.4 ± 3.4 µM, respectively)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: Side chain length at E698 and E701 is not critical for calcium binding.
source: Charge-preserving mutations in E698D and E701D resulted in only a 3 to 10-fold increase in channel EC50 (3.3 ± 0.9 µM and 10.4 ± 3.4 µM, respectively), suggesting that side chain length at these two positions is not critical for calcium binding
evidence: This claim is based on inference from mutagenesis data.

claim: D734E mutation shifted the EC50 by about 800-fold to 0.8 ± 0.3 mM.
source: while mutations in D734E shifted the EC50 by about 800-fold to 0.8 ± 0.3 mM, suggesting that calcium binding may be sensitive to the precise spatial arrangement of the carboxylate group at this position.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: Calcium binding may be sensitive to the precise spatial arrangement of the carboxylate group at position D734.
source: while mutations in D734E shifted the EC50 by about 800-fold to 0.8 ± 0.3 mM, suggesting that calcium binding may be sensitive to the precise spatial arrangement of the carboxylate group at this position.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from mutagenesis data.

claim: E698Q mutation resulted in a relatively small decrease in calcium sensitivity (EC50: 0.03 ± 0.01 mM).
source: E698Q mutations resulted in a relatively small decrease in calcium sensitivity (EC50: 0.03 ± 0.01 mM)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: E701Q and D734N mutations had larger effects on calcium sensitivity (EC50: 2.9 ± 0.3 mM and 2.3 ± 0.3 mM, respectively).
source: while E701Q and D734N had larger effects (EC50: 2.9 ± 0.3 mM and 2.3 ± 0.3 mM, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: Side chain carboxylate groups at position E698, E701 and D734 might be directly involved in binding calcium.
source: This data, combined with a dramatic loss of calcium sensitivity in mutants containing arginine, alanine or cysteine mutations at these three sites, supports the idea that side chain carboxylate groups at position E698, E701 and D734 might be directly involved in binding calcium.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Calcium ions may interact with E730, although not necessarily with its side-chain carboxylate moiety.
source: Similarly, mutagenesis of E730 suggests that calcium ions may interact with this residue, although not necessarily with its side-chain carboxylate moiety (Figure 4D,F).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4D,F.

claim: E730D mutation increased EC50 to 0.8 ± 0.2 mM while E730Q mutation only increased EC50 to 0.09 ± 0.08 mM.
source: In this case, charge-preserving aspartate mutations increased EC50 to 0.8 ± 0.2 mM even though charge-neutralizing glutamine mutations only increased EC50 to 0.09 ± 0.08 mM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: TMEM16A-calcium interactions require the proper conformation of residues at position E730, possibly to orient the carbonyl oxygen of the peptide backbone.
source: Since channels bearing mutations that preserve the shape but not the charge of this acidic residue are more sensitive to calcium, it appears that TMEM16A-calcium interactions require the proper conformation of residues at this position, possibly to orient the carbonyl oxygen of the peptide backbone.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from mutagenesis data.

claim: E650D mutation increased EC50 to 0.8 ± 0.2 mM and E650Q mutation increased EC50 to 4.3 ± 0.9 mM.
source: In contrast to the mild effects of a charge-reversing arginine substitution (EC50: 6.5 ± 0.8 μM), the charge-preserving aspartate and charge-neutralizing glutamine substitutions increased EC50 to 0.8 ± 0.2 mM and 4.3 ± 0.9 mM, respectively
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: Neither the carboxylate nor the carbonyl group of E650 is involved in calcium coordination.
source: suggesting that neither its carboxylate nor its carbonyl group is involved in calcium coordination.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from mutagenesis data.

claim: E650 might be involved in gating processes downstream of calcium binding while E698, E701, E730, and D734 may interact directly with calcium.
source: It thus seems likely that E650 might be involved in gating processes downstream of calcium binding while E698, E701, E730, and D734 may interact directly with calcium.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from mutagenesis data.

claim: Strontium ions can robustly activate TMEM16A channels.
source: Strontium ions can robustly activate TMEM16A channels (Yuan et al., 2013; Ni et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Wildtype TMEM16A channels have a strontium sensitivity with EC50 of 7.7 ± 0.3 μM.
source: Compared to the low micromolar strontium sensitivity (EC50: 7.7 ± 0.3 μM) of wildtype channels (Figure 5A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: E698A and E701A mutations increased the EC50 of channel activation by strontium to at least the hundred micromolar range (EC50: 750 ± 70 μM and 7.6 ± 1.0 mM, respectively).
source: alanine mutations at E698 and E701 increased the EC50 of channel activation by strontium to at least the hundred micromolar range (EC50: 750 ± 70 μM and 7.6 ± 1.0 mM, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from strontium activation studies.

claim: The strontium sensitivity of TMEM16A-CaCCs was drastically reduced by charge-reversing arginine mutations at E698 and E701 (EC50: >10 mM at both sites).
source: The strontium sensitivity of TMEM16A-CaCCs was drastically reduced by charge-reversing arginine mutations (EC50: >10 mM at both sites)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from strontium activation studies.

claim: Strontium sensitivity was partially preserved by charge-preserving aspartate or glutamate mutations at E698 and E701 (EC50: 70 ± 20 μM and 90 ± 10 μM, respectively).
source: and was partially preserved by charge-preserving aspartate or glutamate mutations (EC50: 70 ± 20 μM and 90 ± 10 μM, respectively) (Figure 5D–H)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D–H.

claim: Side chain charge is important for divalent cation coordination at E698 and E701.
source: confirming the importance of side chain charge in divalent cation coordination at these two sites.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from strontium activation data.

claim: Charge-preserving glutamate mutants of D734 are more sensitive to strontium ions than alanine, cysteine, and arginine mutants.
source: Although we were not able to accurately estimate the true EC50 of any D734 mutants because channel activity was too low to properly normalize current amplitude even at 10 mM strontium, it appears that charge-preserving glutamate mutants are more sensitive to strontium ions than alanine, cysteine, and arginine mutants, which were not activated by strontium at all (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: D734 alanine, cysteine, and arginine mutants were not activated by strontium at all.
source: it appears that charge-preserving glutamate mutants are more sensitive to strontium ions than alanine, cysteine, and arginine mutants, which were not activated by strontium at all (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: TMEM16A's apparent EC50 for strontium activation depends more on the physical conformation of the side chain than the presence of a carboxylate moiety at residue 730.
source: Similar to our observations of calcium-dependent channel activation (Figure 4D), TMEM16A's apparent EC50 for strontium activation seems to depend more on the physical conformation of the side chain than the presence of a carboxylate moiety at residue 730.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from strontium activation data.

claim: E730D channels (EC50: 0.27 ± 0.03 mM) are not much more sensitive to strontium than E730A channels (EC50: 0.44 ± 0.10 mM).
source: Channels containing a charge-preserving aspartate mutation at E730 (EC50: 0.27 ± 0.03 mM) are not much more sensitive to strontium than channels containing a charge-neutralizing alanine mutation (EC50: 0.44 ± 0.10 mM) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: E730D mutant channel had the highest sensitivity for strontium out of the five mutations tested at that position.
source: Channels containing the aspartate substitution (E730D) had the highest sensitivity for strontium out of the five mutations tested (Figure 5H)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: E730D mutant channel had the lowest affinity for calcium among E730 mutants.
source: even though the same mutant channel had the lowest affinity for calcium (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The smaller aspartate side chain at position E730 can accommodate the larger strontium ion more easily, supporting its direct interaction with these divalent cations.
source: It is conceivable that the smaller aspartate side chain at this position can accommodate the larger strontium ion more easily, supporting its direct interaction with these divalent cations.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the structural basis for the observed data.

claim: E650 is not directly involved in metal ion binding.
source: In contrast to E698, E701, E730, and D734 that display features consistent with their direct interaction with calcium and strontium ions, the effects of the E650 mutations on channel activation by strontium (Figure 5C) further support the notion that E650 is not directly involved in metal ion binding, as indicated by their effects on calcium sensitivity (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from strontium and calcium activation data.

claim: E650R mutant channel exhibited the highest sensitivity to strontium among E650 mutants and was the only substitution at that site that yielded an EC50 for strontium below 10 mM.
source: Among all of the channels with mutations at residue 650 from which we could observe strontium-activated currents, the charge-reversing E650R mutant channel exhibited the highest sensitivity to strontium and was the only substitution at that site that yielded an EC50 for strontium below 10 mM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from strontium activation studies.

claim: Arginine substitutions of E698 and E730 exhibited the lowest strontium sensitivity as compared to other mutations of these residues.
source: In contrast, arginine substitutions of E698 and E730 exhibited the lowest strontium sensitivity as compared to other mutations of these residues
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from strontium activation studies.

claim: Arginine substitutions of E701 and D734 raised EC50 for strontium beyond 10 mM.
source: and arginine substitutions of E701 and D734 raised EC50 for strontium beyond 10 mM (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: E650 probably plays an indirect role in channel activation by divalent cations and its side chain is likely involved in an allosteric activation mechanism downstream of metal ion binding.
source: This is further evidence that E650 probably plays an indirect role in channel activation by divalent cations and that its side chain is likely involved in an allosteric activation mechanism downstream of metal ion binding.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from strontium activation data.

claim: Cadmium is a divalent cation that is able to substitute for calcium and activate wildtype TMEM16A channels.
source: Cadmium, with an ionic radius of 0.97 Å that is slightly smaller than that of strontium and calcium, is a divalent cation that is able to substitute for calcium and activate wildtype TMEM16A channels (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Cadmium is a 'soft' ligand typically coordinated by only four residues.
source: Unlike calcium and strontium ions, however, cadmium is a 'soft' ligand typically coordinated by only four residues (Dudev et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established chemical knowledge.

claim: Cadmium prefers coordination by moieties containing nitrogen and sulfur atoms.
source: and it prefers coordination by moieties containing nitrogen and sulfur atoms (Andersen, 1984; Sóvágó and Várnagy, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established chemical knowledge.

claim: The TMEM16A calcium-binding site is evolutionarily optimized for 'hard' ions like calcium.
source: Reasoning that the TMEM16A calcium-binding site is evolutionarily optimized for 'hard' ions like calcium, we hypothesized that the TMEM16A sensitivity for cadmium ions would be low and would not be greatly impacted by mutations that alter the charge of only one acidic residue in the calcium sensor.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about evolutionary optimization.

claim: Cadmium (EC50: 940 ± 80 μM) is much less effective than calcium (EC50: 1.0 ± 0.1 μM) and strontium (EC50: 7.7 ± 0.3 μM) at activating the wildtype TMEM16A channel.
source: Indeed, cadmium (EC50: 940 ± 80 μM) is much less effective than calcium (EC50: 1.0 ± 0.1 μM) and strontium (EC50: 7.7 ± 0.3 μM) at activating the wildtype TMEM16A channel (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: TMEM16A channels were poorly activated by 100 μM cadmium even though it reaches its maximum open probability at 100 μM calcium and 100 μM strontium.
source: TMEM16A channels were poorly activated by 100 μM cadmium even though it reaches its maximum open probability at 100 μM calcium (Figure 1C) and 100 μM strontium (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C, 5B, and 6.

claim: E650R mutation caused a slight left-shift of the dose response curve of cadmium activation.
source: The charge-reversing E650R mutation caused a slight left-shift of the dose response curve of cadmium activation (Figure 6C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mutations of E698, E701, E730, and D734 shifted the EC50 of cadmium activation.
source: Although mutations of E698, E701, E730, and D734 shifted the EC50 of cadmium activation, the differences in EC50 between different mutants (Figure 6D–G) were much smaller than those observed with calcium and strontium (Figure 4B–E, Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: The EC50s for cadmium activation of TMEM16A channels containing charge-reversing or charge-neutralizing mutations of E698, E701, E730, and D734 were all in the millimolar range.
source: It is worth noting that the EC50s for cadmium activation of TMEM16A channels containing charge-reversing or charge-neutralizing mutations of these acidic residues were all in the millimolar range, similar to those of wildtype channels and those with charge-preserving mutations (Figure 6H)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The binding of cadmium ions is not as sensitive as the binding of calcium or strontium ions to side chain perturbations of just one of the putative calcium binding residues.
source: suggesting that the binding of cadmium ions is not as sensitive as the binding of calcium or strontium ions to side chain perturbations of just one of these putative calcium binding residues.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cadmium activation data.

claim: The difference in sensitivity to mutations reflects the difference in coordination chemistry between the soft cadmium ion and the harder calcium and strontium ions.
source: This may reflect the difference in coordination chemistry between the soft cadmium ion and the harder calcium and strontium ions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from chemical knowledge and experimental data.

claim: Calcium, strontium, and cadmium activation of TMEM16A-CaCC are all affected by mutations of E698, E701, E730, and D734.
source: Since calcium, strontium, and cadmium activation of TMEM16A-CaCC are all affected by mutations of E698, E701, E730, and D734, it appears that all three divalent cations can interact with the same TMEM16A calcium sensor.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data with multiple divalent cations.

claim: All three divalent cations (calcium, strontium, and cadmium) can interact with the same TMEM16A calcium sensor.
source: Since calcium, strontium, and cadmium activation of TMEM16A-CaCC are all affected by mutations of E698, E701, E730, and D734, it appears that all three divalent cations can interact with the same TMEM16A calcium sensor.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data with multiple divalent cations.

claim: The TMEM16A polypeptide itself encodes the calcium sensor responsible for channel activation.
source: In addition, because all of our mutations targeted residues on TMEM16A, our results lend further support to the notion that the TMEM16A polypeptide itself encodes the calcium sensor responsible for channel activation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the mutagenesis data.

claim: E698, E701, E730, and D734 are exposed to the cytoplasm.
source: Our results implicating E698, E701, E730, and D734 as divalent cation coordinating residues in the TMEM16A calcium-sensing domain suggest that these acidic residues are exposed to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the functional data.

claim: The activity of TMEM16A channels containing an E701C/E730C double mutation can be modulated by the redox potential of the internal solution.
source: the perfusion of internal solutions containing redox chemicals and 300 μM calcium altered the amplitude of chloride currents through channels containing an E701C/E730C double mutation but not those containing an E701C or an E730C single mutation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from redox manipulation experiments.

claim: Channel activity of E701C/E730C double mutant in oxidizing conditions was significantly smaller than those recorded in reducing conditions.
source: Channel activity in oxidizing conditions was significantly smaller than those recorded in reducing conditions, suggesting that formation of a disulfide bridge between E701C and E730C decreases TMEM16A-CaCC activation by calcium (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Formation of a disulfide bridge between E701C and E730C decreases TMEM16A-CaCC activation by calcium.
source: Channel activity in oxidizing conditions was significantly smaller than those recorded in reducing conditions, suggesting that formation of a disulfide bridge between E701C and E730C decreases TMEM16A-CaCC activation by calcium (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from redox manipulation data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: E701 and E730 are spatially clustered at a cytoplasm-accessible site.
source: Thus, these residues appear to be spatially clustered at a cytoplasm-accessible site.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the disulfide bridge formation data.

claim: Calmodulin is not responsible for calcium activation of TMEM16A-CaCC.
source: Our study is in agreement with the conclusions of Terashima et al. (2013) and Yu et al. (2014) that calmodulin is not involved in the calcium-dependent activation of TMEM16A channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to other studies.

claim: Mutations of four putative calcium binding residues E698, E701, E730, and D734 differentially shifted the EC50 of channel activation to different calcium concentrations depending on the size and charge of the amino acid side chains.
source: Moreover, mutations of four putative calcium binding residues E698, E701, E730, and D734 differentially shifted the EC50 of channel activation to different calcium concentrations depending on the size and charge of the amino acid side chains, suggesting that these residues are likely involved in binding calcium.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: E698, E701, E730, and D734 are likely involved in binding calcium.
source: Moreover, mutations of four putative calcium binding residues E698, E701, E730, and D734 differentially shifted the EC50 of channel activation to different calcium concentrations depending on the size and charge of the amino acid side chains, suggesting that these residues are likely involved in binding calcium.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from mutagenesis data.

claim: The differences in the way mutations affect channel sensitivity to hard calcium and strontium ions versus softer cadmium ions suggest that these mutations directly impact channel–ion interactions rather than acting via an allosteric mechanism.
source: Furthermore, the differences in the way these mutations affect channel sensitivity to the hard calcium and strontium ions and the softer cadmium ions suggest that these mutations directly impact channel–ion interactions rather than acting via an allosteric mechanism.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data with multiple divalent cations.

claim: CaM may physically interact with TMEM16A channels under certain conditions.
source: It remains possible that CaM may physically interact with TMEM16A channels under certain conditions as evidenced by previous biochemical studies (Jung et al., 2013; Vocke et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and citations to previous biochemical studies.

claim: The CaM-TMEM16A interaction, if present, is not responsible for the calcium-dependent activation of TMEM16A-CaCC channels.
source: Nevertheless, this interaction, if present, is not responsible for the calcium-dependent activation of TMEM16A-CaCC channels.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Calcium directly binds to and activates TMEM16A-CaCC channels in a fashion reminiscent of the calcium activation mechanism of the BK potassium channel.
source: It seems likely that calcium directly binds to and activates TMEM16A-CaCC channels in a fashion reminiscent of the calcium activation mechanism of the large conductance, calcium-activated BK potassium channel, one of the most well-characterized calcium-activated ion channels.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparison with BK channels.

claim: Both TMEM16A and BK channels contain calcium binding sites that are composed of multiple intracellular acidic residues.
source: Both channels contain calcium binding sites that are composed of multiple intracellular acidic residues, and substitution mutagenesis studies of both channels reveal that side chain properties are critical to the binding of calcium and other metal ions such as strontium, barium, and cadmium.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of BK channels and experimental data from TMEM16A.

claim: Removing carboxylate groups from side chains dramatically reduces or eliminates the ability of both TMEM16A and BK channels to bind calcium.
source: Removing carboxylate groups from side chains dramatically reduces or eliminates the ability of both channels to bind calcium, while preserving carboxylate groups with charge-conserving mutations tends to partially rescue calcium sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from TMEM16A and knowledge of BK channels.

claim: BK channels have three distinct metal binding sites in the pore-forming subunit.
source: There are three distinct metal binding sites in the pore-forming subunit of BK channels (Schreiber and Salkoff, 1997; Shi et al., 2002; Xia et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies of BK channels.

claim: The apparent calcium and strontium sensitivities of TMEM16A-CaCC are similar to that of the high affinity cation binding sites in BK channels.
source: For TMEM16A-CaCC, the apparent calcium (EC50: 1.0 ± 0.1 μM) and strontium (EC50: 7.7 ± 0.3 μM) sensitivities are similar to that of the high affinity cation binding sites in BK channels.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental data with knowledge of BK channels.

claim: The TMEM16A channel is much less sensitive to barium (EC50: 330 ± 30 μM) and cadmium (EC50: 940 ± 80 μM) than BK channels.
source: However, the TMEM16A channel is much less sensitive to barium (EC50: 330 ± 30 μM) and cadmium (EC50: 940 ± 80 μM) than BK channels, which responds to 10 μM barium and cadmium via the calcium bowl and the RCK1 high affinity site, respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental data with knowledge of BK channels.

claim: The high affinity calcium binding site(s) in the TMEM16A channel might be less effective in binding barium and cadmium ions due to their less optimal coordination chemistry.
source: This difference suggests that the high affinity calcium binding site(s) in the TMEM16A channel might be less effective in binding barium and cadmium ions due to their less optimal coordination chemistry.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the structural basis for the observed differences.

claim: Barium and/or cadmium might activate the TMEM16A channel via an unknown low affinity cation binding site.
source: Alternatively, barium and/or cadmium might activate the TMEM16A channel via an unknown low affinity cation binding site, which remains latent under physiological conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: None of the high affinity site mutations abolishes cadmium activation.
source: This scenario seems plausible as none of our high affinity site mutations abolishes cadmium activation (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The high affinity calcium binding residues of TMEM16A channels are between the putative transmembrane segments 5 and 7.
source: Unlike the high affinity sites of BK channels that are located at the large cytosolic C-terminus (Salkoff et al., 2006), the high affinity calcium binding residues (E698, E701, E730, and D734) of the TMEM16A channels are between the putative transmembrane (TM) segments 5 and 7 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data and comparison with BK channels.

claim: The third intracellular loop (between TM6′ and TM7) is important for the calcium sensitivity of the TMEM16A and TMEM16B CaCC channels.
source: This is consistent with recent findings (Yu et al., 2012; Scudieri et al., 2013) that the third intracellular loop (between TM6′ and TM7, Figure 7C, Model B) is important for the calcium sensitivity of the TMEM16A and TMEM16B CaCC channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Residues 701 and 730 are accessible to the intracellular solvent and are in close proximity such that a disulfide bridge can form between E701C and E730C.
source: Our current study provides new insight into the membrane topology of this region by showing that residues 701 and 730 are accessible to the intracellular solvent and are in close proximity such that a disulfide bridge can form between E701C and E730C to impact calcium activation of the channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from disulfide bridge formation experiments.

claim: The hydrophobic region spanning 28 residues (including the putative TM6″) between E701 and E730 likely forms a short reentrant loop.
source: This functional study implies that the hydrophobic region spanning 28 residues (including the putative TM6″) between E701 and E730 likely forms a short reentrant loop (Model C in Figure 7C), bringing together these four acidic residues at both ends of this loop to coordinate calcium ions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the disulfide bridge formation data.

claim: The putative calcium binding acidic residues are highly conserved among proteins in the TMEM16 family.
source: Interestingly, these putative calcium binding acidic residues are highly conserved among proteins in the TMEM16 family, some of which have been shown to be important in cellular processes ranging from mucus secretion (Huang et al., 2012b) to blood coagulation (Suzuki et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2012) in mammals and host defense in Drosophila (Wong et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The identification of evolutionarily conserved acidic residues that bind calcium in TMEM16A-CaCC will contribute towards a general understanding of the molecular mechanisms of calcium-activated TMEM16 channels.
source: The identification of these evolutionarily conserved acidic residues that bind calcium in the TMEM16A-CaCC channel will contribute towards a general understanding of the molecular mechanisms of calcium-activated TMEM16 channels as well as their cellular functions in response to calcium signaling in various cell types and organisms.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the broader implications of the findings.
